supplement.holds: The main PDF refers to SI Section A and Fig. S1 for detailed design/materials; B1.3 for examples; B3.2 for evaluation dimensions; B3.1/B4.1 for evaluator demographics; Tables S1-S2 for model-output quality, S3-S4 for participant descriptives/balance, S5 for human email-quality regressions, S6 for interrater reliability, S7-S8 for prompt-length checks, S9 for email length, S10 for writing time, S11-S12 for confidence/difficulty, and S13 for task-type heterogeneity (pp. 2-6). These SI materials are absent from the ten-page PDF. Their coefficients, descriptive statistics, numerical standard errors, and observation counts have not been inspected. During finalization, requests to the Europe PMC full-text and PMC Open Access APIs failed with WinError 10013 (socket access forbidden); the linked Figshare data were also inaccessible for the same reason.

paper_design_summary: Study 1 evaluates 600 GPT-4-generated business recommendations in English, Arabic, and Chinese, without a human-production comparison (p. 2, Methods). Study 2 reports 480 email writers and describes random assignment to supplied GPT-4 recommendations or no AI-generated content; evaluators rated creativity, completeness, relevance, and actionability, and the analysis also measured email length (pp. 2-3, Methods and Statistical analysis; p. 6, productivity results). The reported participant counts are not explicitly identified as analyzed counts after the attention-check and completion-time filters, so those counts remain unconfirmed (p. 2, overview and Methods; p. 3, sample-inclusion rule).

studies.label: Study 1: evaluation of AI-generated business recommendations

assignment.what_was_assigned: No people were assigned to AI assistance. GPT-4 responses to business prompts were evaluated across English, Arabic, and Chinese (p. 2, Methods).
assignment.quote: ChatGPT-4 was then used to generate responses to each prompt in all three languages, resulting in 600 AI-generated responses (200 prompts × 3 languages).

participants.who: The production sample consists of 600 AI-generated responses to 200 business prompts in three languages. Six native-speaker evaluators, two per language, had relevant business-domain experience; they are raters, not people producing creative work or receiving AI assistance (p. 2, Methods).
participants.quote: a team of six native speakers (two for each language) with prior experience in the relevant business domains were recruited.

ai_tool.how_used: Generated business recommendations in English, Arabic, and Chinese for evaluation; no human-authored comparison outputs (p. 2, Methods).

task.description: AI responses to common business issues in marketing, customer service, human resources, and R&D were rated for Completeness, Relevance, Actionability, and Creativity (p. 2, Methods).

studies.label: Study 2: randomized business-email writing; RCT setting not stated

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual participants were randomly assigned to receive a pre-generated GPT-4 response with the email-writing task or to write without AI-generated content (p. 2, Methods). Assistance is a between-person treatment; language is a participant-group characteristic, not a reported randomized assignment. The main PDF does not identify a laboratory, an online panel, or an ordinary-work/coursework setting, so design_class remains other (p. 2, Methods; p. 9, Limitations).
assignment.quote: The participants were randomly assigned to either a treatment group, wherein they were provided with AI-generated content to assist their writing of an email to address a hypothetical business issue;
assignment.locator: p. 2, Methods, Study 2 paragraph; p. 2, Research motivation and overview
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 3, Methods continuation: https://osf.io/u7s2g; the registration itself was not inspected

arms.name: AI-generated content
arms.description: Pregenerated ChatGPT-4 business recommendations were presented as text directly under the task instruction and could assist the email. The paper reports 240 treated participants across the three languages (p. 2, Research motivation and overview). This reported group size is not explicitly identified as the analyzed count after the attention-check and completion-time filters (p. 3, Methods continuation).

arms.name: Control without AI-generated content
arms.description: Write the business email as in a typical work setting, without using AI-generated content. The paper reports 240 participants in this group across the three languages (p. 2, Research motivation and overview; Methods). This reported group size is not explicitly identified as the analyzed count after the attention-check and completion-time filters (p. 3, Methods continuation).

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 480 human participants (160 per language; p. 2, Methods), with 240 shown AI content and 240 not shown it (p. 2, Research motivation and overview). It states: "The sample includes all responses that passed the attention check and in which participants took more than the 15-minute suggested time." (p. 3, Methods continuation). The main PDF does not explicitly identify the reported totals as the analyzed counts after these filters. The analyzed total and arm counts are therefore null. The initial recruitment/assignment counts and numbers excluded are not separately reported; n_randomized remains null. No intention-to-treat claim is made. SI Section A, Fig. S1, and Tables S3-S5, or participant-level data, are needed to establish the participant flow and verify at least 50 analyzed people.
participants.who: People proficient in English, Arabic, or Chinese; the paper reports 160 per language without explicitly identifying this as the analyzed count after exclusions (p. 2, Methods; p. 3, sample-inclusion rule). Recruitment source and occupational sampling frame are not stated in the main PDF, so population remains null. Within-language arm counts are not printed and were not obtained by dividing the language totals.
participants.country: Not stated. The paper describes participants as spread across the world (p. 9, Limitations); language groups are not treated as countries.
participants.quote: Specifically, a preregistered experiment was implemented, which involved 480 human participants (160 per language) proficient in English, Arabic, or Chinese.
participants.locator: p. 2, Research motivation and overview and Methods; p. 3, sample inclusion rule; p. 9, Limitations

ai_tool.how_used: GPT-4 recommendations from Study 1 were supplied as text directly below the task instructions during email writing (p. 2, overview and Methods). The supplied content was available when the scored email was produced. The paper describes pre-generated responses instead of repeated interaction with an LLM (p. 9, Limitations). Model snapshot and generation settings are not given in the main PDF.

task.description: Write an email addressing a hypothetical business issue in marketing, customer service, human resources, or R&D. The emails propose solutions/recommendations and are explicitly scored for creativity along with completeness, relevance, and actionability (pp. 2-3, Methods). R&D tasks concern new technologies and products (p. 6, Task types).
task.duration: 15-minute suggested time; the stated analysis inclusion rule requires more than that time (p. 3, Methods continuation). No fixed maximum or later-session assessment is reported.

outcomes.name: Email Creativity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Six trained evaluators rated the human-written emails (p. 2, Methods). The main PDF identifies trained evaluators but does not establish whether they meet the codebook category for lay raters/crowd workers or for experts/professionals; measure remains null pending SI B4.1 (p. 2, overview and Methods; p. 9, Limitations; creativity-codebook.md, section 6). Figure 1 displays a 1-5 rating scale (pp. 4-5); full anchors require SI B3.2. The paper defines Y_i as the rating of email i and states that model standard errors were clustered at participant level (p. 3, Statistical analysis). It does not say whether regression rows contain individual evaluator ratings or evaluator-averaged email scores; unit and n_units remain null pending the rating-aggregation protocol and SI Table S5. Creativity concerns multiple suggestions outside the creative repertoire of the average manager (p. 3, Methods). Task-type moderation reports less creative Chinese R&D emails relative to the marketing baseline (p = 0.025; p. 6, Task types; external SI Table S13); Fig. 3 on p. 8 displays creativity for R&D and non-R&D tasks. The paper explicitly names this dimension among its primary email-quality outcomes (p. 3, Statistical analysis); preregistered primary status was not independently checked. Prompt-length variants are discussed on pp. 4-5 with SI Tables S7-S8. Demographic/experience heterogeneity, ordered-logit specifications, and control-variable checks are summarized on p. 6 without coefficients. These are variants of this outcome, not separate outcome entries.

contrasts.reported: Figure 1(d) shows a higher AI-treatment median than control within each language. No numerical within-language AI-versus-control coefficient, arm mean/SD, SE, confidence interval, or p-value is printed in the main PDF. The relevant regression table is external SI Table S5; no values were estimated from boxplot positions.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Fig. 1(d), Creativity; p. 3, AI effects on the quality of human work across languages (Study 2), reference to SI Table S5

contrasts.reported: Chinese versus English: "0.49 standard deviations less Creativity (p = 0.016)". This is the difference between language-specific AI treatment effects, not a direct AI-versus-control effect or a comparison of the treated groups alone. The standardizing SD and the coefficient SE are not given in the main text.
contrasts.locator: p. 3, AI effects on the quality of human work across languages (Study 2); Statistical analysis, specification (2); SI Table S5 referenced but absent

outcomes.name: Email length (normalized characters)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Direct email length measured as the number of normalized characters (p. 6, AI effects on productivity across languages). The metric itself is explicit. The supplied measure vocabulary has no direct character-count category, and the paper does not report lexical overlap or a creativity-scoring model for this outcome; the measure code remains null pending an approved vocabulary mapping. It is an elaboration outcome, not an across-person diversity measure. The normalization procedure, arm means/SDs, and regression observation counts are absent from the main PDF. All model standard errors are described as clustered at participant level (p. 3, Statistical analysis). Task-type moderation reports shorter R&D emails in Arabic and Chinese relative to marketing (p = 0.037 and 0.020, respectively; p. 6, Task types; SI Table S13). The p_value_only flags record the only printed precision information; raw increases and percentage changes are also retained in reported.

eligibility.reason: Study 2 explicitly randomly assigned individual people to supplied GPT-4 content versus no AI-generated assistance for email writing (p. 2, Methods), and trained evaluators rated creativity on the emails produced (pp. 2-3, Methods and creativity rubric). The main text reports 480 people, 160 per language, and assistance groups of 240 each (p. 2, overview and Methods), but does not explicitly connect these counts to the sample retained after the attention-check and more-than-15-minute inclusion rule (p. 3, Methods continuation). Under form-spec.md, criterion 2 counts analyzed people across arms. The analyzed total and arm counts are unconfirmed, so criterion 2 and core eligibility are unclear; the evidence does not establish fewer than 50 people. The external supplement and linked data could not be inspected because requests failed with WinError 10013. Rater-category, setting, and rating-aggregation uncertainties do not change the verified random-assignment and output-scoring criteria. Study 1 is model_only and supplies no eligible human-assistance sample.

one_line_finding: The AI-assistance effect on email creativity was 0.49 standard deviations smaller in Chinese than in English (p = 0.016; p. 3, Study 2 quality results); the analyzed participant count is unconfirmed (pp. 2-3, Methods).
open_questions: For each of the four rated quality outcomes, inspect the rating-aggregation protocol and SI Table S5 to distinguish individual evaluator-rating rows from evaluator-averaged email-score rows. The main text does not resolve output versus rating as the analysis unit.

The email-length metric is confirmed as normalized character count, but no supplied measure code describes it exactly. An approved codebook mapping or a direct length/count category is needed; lexical_overlap would misdescribe the measure. This is an Atlas vocabulary issue; no further source evidence is needed to confirm that the metric counts normalized characters.

The external SI is needed to establish the RCT setting and recruitment population, initial assignment count, exclusions, analyzed total and arm counts, and per-language arm counts. The reported 480-person study sample is not explicitly linked to the post-filter analyzed sample (pp. 2-3, Methods). Confirm the number of distinct analyzed writers across all arms to settle criterion 2.

SI Table S5 is needed for numerical within-language AI-versus-control coefficients, arm descriptives, numerical SEs, observation counts, and the standardizer underlying the printed standard-deviation differences between language-specific treatment effects.

SI B4.1/B3.2 and Table S9 are needed for evaluator qualifications, complete scale anchors, the character-normalization procedure, and email-length regression uncertainty. The four rated outcomes retain null measure codes until evaluator qualifications establish the lay/crowd-worker or expert/professional category; the fact that evaluators scored the produced emails is already confirmed.
The article reports an OSF preregistration, but it was not inspected; retain paper_primary rather than assert preregistered_primary.
notes: Finalized on 2026-10-09. Read the complete 306-line markdown in successive chunks, including references and end matter, and extracted all ten PDF pages with PyMuPDF. The PDF contains no appended supplement or embedded attachments. Figure 1 on pp. 4-5 was rendered and visually inspected in memory to check its 1-5 scales and qualitative median directions. All retained numerical results were checked against the PDF; no effect sizes, standard errors, participant counts, or numerical figure values were calculated. Values printed as p = 0.000 remain as printed. All four challenge problems were corrected: one rater-category problem spanning four outcomes, and three unsupported analyzed-count entries. The reported 480 total, 160 per language, and 240 per assistance group remain descriptive source statements; none is asserted to be a verified count after exclusions. The analyzed total and arm counts are null, and sample-size eligibility is unclear. n_open counts unresolved challenge decisions; the remaining evidentiary uncertainties are listed separately in final.open_items. Study 1 reports model-output evaluations and no human-assistance or human-production comparison, so its outcomes array remains empty. Study 2 retains creativity, completeness, relevance, actionability, and email length. Writing time is a process outcome; confidence and perceived difficulty are self-reports. No across-person diversity or post-removal outcome is reported. Cross-language treatment-effect differences are other contrasts, not within-language ai_vs_bau effects or randomized language comparisons. Direct AI-versus-control quality results are figure-only in the supplied PDF. Task-type and robustness variants remain within their parent outcomes. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the historical record; its earlier analyzed-count confirmations and sample-size eligibility judgment are superseded by the current fields and final object. All five unresolved reconciliation differences are covered by final.open_items. Finalization retrieval used Python urllib with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC12373962/fullTextXML, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/utils/oa/oa.fcgi?id=PMC12373962, and https://figshare.com/s/b27991ce8ea36143d7ef. All three requests failed with WinError 10013 (socket access forbidden). No supplementary material or posted data was read or saved. The OSF registration was not independently inspected; paper_primary is retained. The data URL is printed on p. 9; no code URL is stated. Only forms/c414.json is written.

S2-O5 email-length measure code (open_questions[1]; reconciliation.differences: studies[S2].outcomes[S2-O5].measure): the normalized-character metric is explicit (p. 6, productivity results). Retain null because the supplied vocabulary has no exact category. An Atlas codebook mapping would settle this administrative issue; no further empirical source is needed.

Study 2 setting and recruitment population (part of open_questions[2]): inspect SI Section A and Tables S3-S4 to choose the RCT setting and population codes. Individual random assignment is already explicit (p. 2, Methods), so the unknown setting does not affect criterion 1.

Study 2 analyzed participant count after exclusions (part of open_questions[2] and all three people challenges): inspect SI Section A, Fig. S1, and Tables S3-S5 for initial assignment, exclusions, retained total and arm counts, and per-language cells. Establish that at least 50 distinct people were analyzed across all arms after the attention-check and more-than-15-minute filters to settle criterion 2; the reported 480 total and 240 per arm do not explicitly settle this (pp. 2-3, Methods). If SI does not resolve the count, participant-level posted data or author clarification is needed.

Quality-effect extraction (open_questions[3]): SI Table S5 is needed for within-language AI-versus-control coefficients, arm descriptives, numerical clustered standard errors, observation counts, and the standardizer underlying the printed differences in standard deviations (p. 3, Statistical analysis and quality results). These quantities affect estimation, not the three eligibility criteria; the unique analyzed-people threshold is tracked separately.

Study 2 evaluator qualifications (part of open_questions[4] and outcome challenge): inspect SI B4.1 to classify S2-O1 through S2-O4 as human_raters or expert_raters. Six trained evaluators and output-based creativity ratings are established (p. 2, Methods); their qualifications affect the measure code, not criterion 3.

Complete quality-rating scale anchors (part of open_questions[4]): inspect SI B3.2. The main text gives the creativity rubric and Figure 1 shows the rating scale, so missing full anchors do not undermine output-scoring eligibility (pp. 3-5).

Email-length normalization and regression uncertainty (part of open_questions[4]): inspect SI Table S9 and associated methods for the normalized-character procedure, arm descriptives, observation counts, and numerical uncertainty (p. 6, productivity results). These details concern the secondary elaboration outcome and do not determine eligibility.

Preregistered outcome priority (open_questions[5]): obtain an accessible copy of the stated OSF preregistration, https://osf.io/u7s2g (p. 3, Methods continuation), or confirmation from the author. Retain paper_primary until the registered outcome hierarchy is checked; preregistration status is not an eligibility criterion.
